# Get started on NuttX in QEMU (Arm)

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: starter status -->
> **Status:** Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry: [`nros-board-nuttx-qemu`](../reference/boards/nuttx-arm.md); [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED starter status -->

This starter puts a talker on Apache NuttX, on QEMU's Arm `virt` machine (a
Cortex-A7), and shows its messages arriving in ROS 2. NuttX is a POSIX-style
RTOS, so the talker runs as an ordinary NuttX task, with NuttX's own network
stack on a virtio-net device. You need no NuttX checkout of your own:
`nros setup` fetches the kernel and its apps tree, and `nros run` links your
node into a bootable kernel. You write the talker in Rust or in C; pick a tab
and every tab on the page follows.

## What you need

- A Linux host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros` is on
  your `PATH`.
- ROS 2 Humble with `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp`. ROS 2 provides the zenoh
  router the board talks to, and the message definitions the build generates
  the talker's code from.
- Two host packages the NuttX kernel build uses, the Python venv module and
  `unzip`. The provision step installs them for you when you allow it.

No board, no cable: QEMU's user-mode network carries the guest's ethernet to
your machine, with no TAP device to create. WiFi is deferred to the Zephyr
4.4 line, so no starter opens over WiFi yet.

## Provision

```bash probe=30
nros setup qemu-armv7a-nuttx --rmw zenoh --sudo
```

That fetches the NuttX cross-compiler, the QEMU that emulates the machine, and
the NuttX kernel and apps sources into a shared store under `~/.nros`. Before
it downloads anything it names the host packages that are missing, and
`--sudo` lets it run the one install command it composed for your package
manager (`sudo apt-get install -y python3-venv unzip` on Debian or Ubuntu).
Leave `--sudo` off and it only prints that command. It installs no router:
the router is ROS's `rmw_zenohd`.

## Scaffold the project

<!-- tabs -->

### Rust

```bash probe=40
nros new nx_ws --board qemu-armv7a-nuttx --template talker --lang rust
cd nx_ws
```

### C

```bash probe=40
nros new nx_ws --board qemu-armv7a-nuttx --template talker --lang c
cd nx_ws
```

<!-- /tabs -->

That wrote a workspace with two packages: `src/nx_node/`, the talker, a
library with no `main()` that names no board, and `src/nx_node_bringup/`,
which says what the talker runs on. The NuttX task that runs your node is
generated from the bringup when you build, so you do not need to open it for
this starter.

## Run it in QEMU

The guest sits on QEMU's user-mode network at `10.0.2.15`, and dials the
router through the gateway `10.0.2.2`, which is your host, on port 7447.
Start the router first, in its own terminal, listening on every interface so
the guest's connection arrives:

<!-- removed when the board descriptor states its default locator -->
```bash probe=50 probe-run=60 probe-keep
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd
```

```text probe-expect=50
Started Zenoh router with id
```

Then, in a second terminal, in the workspace, source ROS 2 and build and run
the talker. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so
later runs of it need no sourced shell:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=1500
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run nx_node --expect 'Publishing:'
```

```text probe-expect=60
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

`nros run` builds the kernel with your node linked in (the first build
configures NuttX from the board's defconfig and takes several minutes; later
builds take seconds), then boots it on QEMU's `virt` machine with virtio-net
on the user-mode network. The image starts its application itself, so what
you see is the talker on the NuttX console. With `--expect` it stops QEMU and
exits 0 at the first console line containing that text, and exits 1 if the
board stops first. The router keeps running.

Without `--expect` it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C, which stops QEMU:

```bash probe=65 probe-run=120 probe-keep
nros run nx_node
```

```text probe-expect=65
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## See it in ROS 2

Leave the router and `nros run` going. In a third terminal:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=120
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=70
data: 'Hello World:
```

The talker publishes best-effort, and `ros2 topic echo` defaults to reliable,
which receives nothing from it. That is why the command asks for best-effort.

## If it doesn't work

- **`nros setup` stops and names `python3-venv` or `unzip`:** you left
  `--sudo` off. Run the command it printed, or run the step again with
  `--sudo`.
- **No `Publishing:` line within a minute of boot:** the talker did not reach
  the router. Its first line usually appears within about six seconds of
  boot. Check that the router listens on `0.0.0.0:7447`: one on `127.0.0.1` is
  out of the guest's reach.
- **`nros run` stops at once and names `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH`:** this shell has
  not sourced ROS 2, and no earlier build of the workspace recorded it.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md).
